title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
body: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LuaLaTeX, drawn in Lua

README 節錄：# florilegium ## Origin The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original. This project was made with the assistance of AI (Claude), and I'm sharing the process I used to bring it to life. ## What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden. Try it in your browser. The playground sets a page as a printer's proof, grows its margin with the same Lua, and hands it back as an SVG, a LaTeX preamble or a Typst page setup. *Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.* Two documents share one package, and two more (`showcase.tex`, `spread.tex`) show what else it does: | | `florilegium.tex` | `florilegium-grow.tex` | |---|---|---| | composition | **authored**: stems, leaves and flowers

title: Arjun-Ingole/hop
body:
Install Linux next to Windows without a USB stick

README 節錄： Install Linux next to Windows without a USB stick. ## What it is hop is a single Windows app that installs Linux alongside Windows. Pick a system, choose a drive, drag to choose how much space it gets, and click Install. There's no USB stick to find and nothing to install first. ## What it does - **Downloads from official sources.** It gets the ISO from the project's own server and verifies its checksum where the project publishes one. You can also use an ISO you already have. - **Makes room safely.** It checks your PC first, and nothing on the disk changes until those checks pass. - **Goes where there's room.** Shrink C: or another drive, use free space, or use a second disk inside the PC. If C: is full, hop suggests a drive that isn't, and the download can go elsewhere too. - **Tells you what to click.** It lists the exact choices to make in the Linux installer. - **Gets you unstuck.** If the PC goes back to Windows, reopening hop explains why and can restart into the BIOS. - **Cleans up after itself.** Undo gives the space back to the drive it came from, and it can also remove another Linux already on the drive. - **Can replace Windows entirely, for Ubuntu, Zorin OS, Debian and Arch.** It's a separate choice with its own warning, and you have to type ERASE. hop only makes the installer, which copies itself to memory so it can erase the disk it started from when you tell it to.
